analysis.one_liner: Caps fossil fuel emissions through carbon permit auctions and pays all the proceeds to Americans as equal quarterly dividends.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in December 2024 with zero cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require companies that bring oil, coal, and natural gas into the U.S. market to buy permits for the carbon dioxide their fuels release when burned. The number of permits would shrink each year, cutting emissions 90% below 2015 levels by 2050. All auction proceeds would go into a trust fund and be paid out equally to every eligible American each quarter, so most households—especially lower-income ones—would receive more than they pay in higher fuel prices. It would also add fees on carbon-intensive imports to keep U.S. manufacturers competitive.
analysis.who_benefits: Every eligible American would receive an equal quarterly dividend from the permit auction proceeds. Because wealthier households use far more fossil fuel energy, most lower- and middle-income households would come out ahead financially. People living near fossil fuel pollution would benefit from provisions requiring co-pollutant reductions and air monitoring in frontline communities, and everyone would benefit from slower climate change and reduced extreme weather costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Most American households, especially lower-income ones

how_it_helps.text: The bill distributes 100% of carbon permit auction proceeds equally to every eligible individual with a valid Social Security number who is lawfully present in the U.S., paid quarterly and excluded from gross income.

The permit supply starts 15% below 2015 emissions in 2025 and declines to 90% below 2015 levels by 2050, with a minimum price of $40 per ton rising $10 each year, guaranteeing the cap falls regardless of demand.

An environmental justice chapter requires that carbon reductions come with commensurate reductions in co-pollutants hitting frontline communities, funds air quality monitoring there, and authorizes the EPA to take additional regulatory measures if those communities' pollution burden does not fall as fast as the carbon targets.

Carbon equivalency fees on imports of steel, cement, aluminum, glass, paper, chemicals, and other carbon-intensive goods would protect U.S. manufacturers from cheaper high-emission imports, with matching payments to U.S. exporters.
The bill explicitly preserves state and federal legal claims against fossil fuel companies for climate damage and deception, including nuisance, negligence, and deceptive-practices claims.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers, importers, and refiners would buy permits for every ton of carbon in the fuels they sell, with penalties of three times the permit price for noncompliance, costs that would be passed through to fuel prices. Heavy users of fossil fuel energy—large households in big homes, frequent flyers, energy-intensive industries—would pay more than their dividend. Companies that fail to surrender permits would face triple-damages penalties that are not tax-deductible.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil, coal, and gas companies and heavy fuel users

drawbacks.text: Consumers would face higher prices for gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity, and energy-intensive industries would face higher production costs; the dividend fully offsets costs only for households that use less than an average share of fossil fuel energy.

The bill relies on annual auctions with a rising $40-per-ton price floor and shrinking permit supply; if enforcement or tracking fails, penalties of only triple the permit price could be treated by large firms as a cost of doing business rather than a reason to cut emissions.
Rebates to exporters under the border adjustment could blunt the program's effectiveness on exported goods, and the international agreement the fee is designed to incentivize does not exist today.
The program would add a new administrative apparatus run by the Treasury and EPA, including identity verification for dividend payments through the Social Security Administration.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is strongly weighted toward ordinary households: every dollar raised at auction flows back out as an equal per-person dividend, which research on carbon pricing consistently shows means lower-income households come out ahead while the highest emitters pay the most. The real costs fall on fossil fuel companies and heavy fuel users, though consumers would feel higher fuel prices before dividends arrive. The environmental justice and border-adjustment provisions address two of the main objections to carbon pricing—uneven pollution burdens and uncompetitive industry—but the bill's aggressive targets (90% below 2015 levels by 2050) would require a faster energy transition than the U.S. has managed under any policy to date, so the execution risk is real.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced two days after the December 2024 lame-duck session began, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never heard from again before the Congress ended three weeks later.

narrative.text: Sen. Van Hollen introduced the bill on December 11, 2024, the final month of the 118th Congress.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, where no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers avoided a rising annual cost on every ton of carbon in their fuels, and no household ever faced the higher fuel prices or received the dividends the bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers, avoiding a carbon cost

for.name: Sen. Chris Van Hollen
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill and the Senate referred it to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill—no hearing, markup, or vote—after its referral on December 11, 2024.

against.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no senator from either party cosponsored the bill, so the partisan shape of potential support is unknown from the record; the only action was its referral to a Democratic-chaired committee that did not act.

industries.industry: Oil, coal, and natural gas producers and importers
industries.note: They would buy permits for every ton of carbon in fuels sold into U.S. markets, starting at a $40-per-ton minimum price that rises $10 yearly, plus triple-price penalties for shortfalls. The bill's defeat spared them this perpetual, escalating cost.

A guaranteed, shrinking annual cap on fossil fuel use would push utilities and consumers toward wind, solar, nuclear, and efficiency products at a pace set in statute. The bill died before any of that demand materialized.

industries.industry: Energy-intensive manufacturers (steel, cement, aluminum, glass, paper, chemicals)
industries.note: They would pay permit-linked costs on their energy use but receive exporter rebates and a fee on high-carbon imports, largely shielding them from foreign competition. The bill's failure left them facing no carbon cost at all.

Fuel prices would rise, but the equal per-person dividend returns the full auction revenue to households, so most people below the average energy-use level would net more money than they paid. No such payments ever occurred.
